# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Pathophysiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive and underdiagnosed infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1,2]. The molecular mechanism involves unstable protein precursors undergoing conformational transitions into insoluble beta-sheet-rich fibrils [3]. Once considered rare, epidemiological studies demonstrate that CA is a major contributor to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [4]. Over 95% of clinical cases are caused by two primary precursor proteins: immunoglobulin light chains in light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, and transthyretin in transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [5,6]. AL amyloidosis is a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by rapid progression and direct light-chain-mediated cardiotoxicity [6]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis results from the dissociation of the hepatic transthyretin homotetramer into amyloidogenic monomers [7]. It exists either as hereditary ATTR (ATTRv) due to pathogenic mutations in the *TTR* gene, or as wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an age-related disease predominantly affecting elderly men [7,8].

### Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Challenges
Early recognition is critical because diagnostic delays remain standard in clinical practice, often leading to advanced heart failure before treatment initiation [9]. Patients typically present with progressive dyspnea and fatigue, but key extracardiac "red flags" are crucial clues [10]. These include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, orthostatic hypotension, and peripheral neuropathy [10,11]. Electrocardiography (ECG) classical findings include low voltage in the limb leads, which is highly discordant with the severe left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy seen on echocardiography, though this discordance is absent in many patients [11].

### Diagnostic Framework and Multimodality Imaging
The diagnostic paradigm has evolved significantly, shifting from tissue biopsy to non-invasive imaging. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) typically reveals concentric LV wall thickening, biatrial enlargement, and a pathognomonic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [12]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides high-resolution tissue characterization. Characteristic CMR findings include diffuse, subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) [13,14], along with significantly elevated native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) fraction, which carry vital prognostic value [15].

When CA is suspected, the immediate next step is the concomitant assessment of serum and urine monoclonal proteins [16,17]. This is done using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and a serum free light chain (FLC) assay [16]. If a monoclonal protein is detected, AL amyloidosis must be ruled out via tissue biopsy (fat pad, bone marrow, or endomyocardial) stained with Congo red, as it represents a hematological emergency with poor survival if untreated [17]. If a monoclonal protein is absent, bone-seeking scintigraphy ($^{99m}\text{Tc}$-pyrophosphate [PYP] or $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid [DPD]) is employed [18,19]. A grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on planar and SPECT imaging has a specificity and positive predictive value approaching 100% for ATTR amyloidosis, effectively bypassing the need for endomyocardial biopsy [20,21]. Genetic sequencing of the *TTR* gene is then mandatory to distinguish ATTRv from ATTRwt [22,23].

### Therapeutic Landscape
Management requires a dual approach: supportive cardiac care and disease-modifying therapy [24,25]. Supportive therapy focuses on fluid control with loop diuretics and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [25]. Traditional heart failure medications, such as beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers, are generally poorly tolerated and may exacerbate hypotension due to the restrictive physiology and fixed stroke volume of the amyloid heart [25].

Disease-modifying therapies have revolutionized prognosis. In AL amyloidosis, treatment targets the underlying plasma cell clone. The combination of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) is the current standard of care, offering rapid, deep hematologic responses [26].

For ATTR amyloidosis, therapies target different stages of transthyretin production [27]. Tafamidis, a TTR stabilizer that prevents tetramer dissociation, was shown in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial to reduce all-cause mortality by 30% and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations by 32% [27]. For patients with ATTRv (and increasingly studied in ATTRwt), hepatic TTR gene silencers such as patisiran (an RNAi therapeutic) [28] and inotersen (an antisense oligonucleotide) [29] have demonstrated profound efficacy in reducing circulating TTR levels and slowing neuropathy progression [28,29,30].

### Conclusion
Cardiac amyloidosis has transitioned from a fatal, underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease. The implementation of non-invasive diagnostic algorithms and the advent of highly effective disease-modifying therapies highlight the importance of early detection and multidisciplinary care.
